Hey guys!

The situation is this: I am currently in mock-up stage. I am arranging things in my sandbox and playing with a new overhead beam arrangement. I am as of yet un-isolated - my sandbox sits atop a sheet of MDF (medium density fiberboard). The laser is on this same surface - lasing into the box through a hole in the side. The MDF is here now because it was the stiffest sheet of anything that I could find. It is my intention to replace the MDF with a sheet of granite which will sit atop some innertubes. I guess I can be fairly certain that this crappy MDF is slowly wilting and god knows the whole arrangement sags a few microns every day.

My finished table (unless this is all one big stupid idea) will be as such: A bed of cinder blocks on the concrete floor, on top of which will be a few innertubes, on top of which will be a sheet of granite, on top of which will be my sandbox and laser. 

I have been for all intents and purposes just playing around with my setup as practice for when the whole she-bang is ready to burn some film, and as an attempt to gain some profiency in setting a spatial filter...

I guess it's possible that this post was a bit pre-emptive as I am not dealing with what will be my final arrangement... Hopefully the granite will be sufficiently rigid to eliminate the wandering I see my beams doing now...

posts.topic_title: How long will YOUR spatial filter stay dialed-in?
posts.author: JohnFP
posts.post_subject: How long will YOUR spatial filter stay dialed-in?
posts.content_md:
Justin, wood moves with changes in temperature and humidy. 

I too am currenly resting my laser, optics and plateholder on 3/4 inch plywood box with no vibration isolation. But I am only doing SBR in DCG. I have a 18" by 18' concrete paving block on the wood table that my object and plateholder set on. When I fire up the laser I let it warm for 20 minutes then usually have to dial the spatial filter back in but I do it without touching the spatial filter. Usually you can tweak the x and y gimbal adjustments on the mirror just prior to the spatial filter and get back to your original spatial filter setting in just a few seconds and quite easily.

Also, even when I had the steel vibration isolation table, I had the laser resting off the table and on a kitchen type counter top. Again I would let the laser warm for 20 minutes and almost always lost the spatial filter settings. But again, I had a mirror just in front of the laser (still off the table on on the counter), and could use that mirror to bring the spatial filter back into alignment without touching the spatial filter. And as a confirmation that my table was indeed stable (all optics on the table remained stable relative to one another), I could adjust that first mirror off the table and just after the laser to allign the reference beam spatial filter and the other two object beam spatial filters would come perfectly into focus also.

Now the kicker is, you don't want to originally allign your spatial filter with that mirror or you may get a funny beam profile. Always remove the lens and pinhole from your spatial filter and insure the beam goes though the spatial filter perpendicularly and hits the plate or object squarely and centered where you want it. Then place the lens in and insure the expanded beam also hits the plate or object squarely and centered at the same spot. Then insert the pinhole. If you do this and come back the next day and the beam has moved off your spatial filter, then you should be safe simply using the mirror described above to readjust the spatial filter. Hope this helps!

posts.post_subject: How long will YOUR spatial filter stay dialed-in?
posts.content_md:
Heyhey, John!

Yah - Time and time again, it seems to boil down to what stuff one has. As much as I would love mirrors on precision gimbals and optics that would actually stay in place, I'm regularly 1/4 paycheck from broke, and am doing my best with small mirrors hot-glued to spray can lids and stuck in sand...

My collimating mirror (or the cardboard disk representing it until the length of 1.5" chrome steel tube arrives that I can epoxy to the back of the parabolic itself) is mounted to a sturdy video cam tripod - allowing me to swing it out of the way when I see fit... -and-

My routine for setting my spatial filter is as such: I align my raw beam to my "twister" just before the SF, which kicks it up then over (at an upward slant). I remove the objective and pinhole, then aim the raw beam so that it skewers the SF coaxially and strikes the center of my collimator (cardboard disk for now), then swing the collimator out of the way and mark the spot on the wall where the beam hits with a piece of black tape. I then thread in the objective. At this point, the big beam on the wall should be pretty much centered around the tape. If it is off a touch, I can shift the SF around a little (it's planted in sand atop spray can lids too) until the expanded beam is centered around the tape. I can swing my collimator back into place to confirm even coverage if I see fit. I now stick a piece of white paper in the sand just after the SF where I will see a bright just-starting-to-expand beam. I now magnet on my pinhole and slide it around by hand until the dot is visible and roughly in the right place. Remove paper and if my cave is dark enough, I should be able to find the spot somewhere near the tape on my wall. X and Y it til it's centered on the tape, then zoom in with Z-axis (making tiny X and Y tweaks here and there) until boom - big soft blob of green on my wall. Swing my collimator back into place, and -in theory- it is evenly covered with reference beam.

Like I was saying - The entire rig is thoroughly Micky Mouse right now - a dry run - proficiency training until I have an authentically rigid surface to set it all on. Yep - that MDF gives up the fight a little bit every day and will presumably blow as blustery a sigh of relief as I will when it is finally replaced. For now I guess I'll just resign myself to blaming the saggy excuse for a surface that the MDF is...

Lawdy lawdy lawdy I'll just have to hope that all this stuff sees fit to stay in place when supported properly by granite...

posts.content_md: I have had to deal with beam walk in gas lasers. The angle between the beam and the case can drift slowly. I usually have a very long path from the laser to the spatial filter in order to avoid back reflections and beam walk can cause me to have to readjust the spatial filter. I have not had this problem with diode lasers and I have not used my c315 enough to know if it is a problem.

posts.author: Jeffrey Weil

posts.content_md:
I would never work in a sand box. The rules are "keep it clean" but at the same time "work in a big box of dirt" Never sounded right to me.

I've made a bunch of tables, nothing magic about it. Forget the granite, better ways to spend your money. Granite will not really be any better for you in your situtation than poured concreat. But concreat is MUCH cheaper and MUCH easier to carry around. Its in bags, not a complete slab.

Get a whole bunch of cynder blocks. If your in the UK, breeze blocks. Same thing. Stack up 3 or 4 on their side to make legs. Build a shallow box on top of that, maybe 2 or 3 inches deep. Put in some rebar and pour the concreat. Put down some inertubes. Remember to put a piece of 2x4 of whatever inside the donut hole so if you loose air the table does not come down and crush the tubes. Build another shallow box on top of that, rebar and concreat.

Now lay a whole bunch of cynderblocks, ON THEIR SIDE so no holes are exposed, and morter them together on the sides. Like building a wall horizontally. Then build another shallow box on top of that. No floor this time, just the sides and pour about 1/2 to 1 inch of concrete on top of that to make a nice surface. That also bonds all the blocks together along with the motar on the sides.

Now you have a choice. Either use weighted bases, I wouldn't, or glue a nice single sheet of steel down and use cheap chinese mag mounts. If you look around you can get them for less than 10 dollars each!!!

Ok, so now for about 200 to 300 dollars you have a REAL table. For another 100 bucks or so you have REAL mag mounts. Each block weights close to 30 pounds. so with a few dozen on top your table will weigh plenty.

I've made hundreds of reflection holograms on a table like this. Work great and no sand drift.

The only problem with it was when I got a newport table I had to take it apart! Not easy, but doable.

 Jeffrey Weil
